readme.text:
**Kuration curates large Physical AI datasets into training-ready data for world
models.** Point it at raw gameplay clips or time-series data or video and Kuration picks the windows worth
training on, writes them as shards, and drops a config alongside so the same run can
be rebuilt.

readme_quick.text:
Runnable quickstart against a small sample dataset bundled with the package — no downloads,
no data of your own required:

```python
from kuration import input
from kuration.sample_data import sample_sessions_path

dataset = (
    input(sample_sessions_path(), time="t", entity="device", hz=1)
    .window(12, stride=6)
    .measure("activity", "std", of="signal")
    .measure("fault_rate", "rate", of="fault")
    .bin("activity", bins=3)
    .bin("fault_rate", bins=2)
    .split(test=1/3)
    .sample("equal", n=12)
    .options(seed=7)
)

print(dataset.explain().render())
dataset.output("out/quickstart-out")
```

The result is a train/test set of shards plus a `config.json` recording the schema
and pipeline so the same run can be rebuilt. Every shard has a SHA-256 checksum in
the manifest, so resume and verification are safe.

overview.text:
Kuration is a dataset curation system for sequential data. It sits between raw collection and
training: it decides which windows should enter a dataset, preserves why they were chosen, and
writes the arrays a training loop consumes.

Start with the [guided quickstart](quickstart.md) if you want to run a pipeline now. This page
builds the mental model and then shows the explicit API used for custom schemas, adapters,
strategies, and output contracts.

pipeline.text:
The primary way to drive the SDK for the common case: no explicit `SchemaSpec`,
no explicit adapter, no raw strategy dict. `kuration.input(...)` sniffs a source, infers a
schema (via [`kuration.core.infer`](#schema-inference-kurationcoreinfer)), and returns an immutable `Pipeline`; every
operator returns a *new* `Pipeline` (nothing is mutated in place); a terminal compiles the
chain into the classic strategy dict and calls the existing engine
(`curate` / `write_dataset` / `dataset_report` / `run_experiment` — see [api.md](api.md)).
The explicit APIs in `strategies.md`/`schema.md`/`adapters.md` remain available for custom and
declarative workflows. Every compiled chain is inspectable via `.describe()` before you run it.

pipeline_example.text:
pipeline = (
    input({"s0": rows0, "s1": rows1}, time="t")   # multi-source in-memory rows
    .window(16)
    .measure("hp")
    .filter("hp", "<=", 50)                        # universal predicate: drop bad windows
    .measure("action_entropy", "entropy", of="action")
    .bin("action_entropy", bins=4)                  # diversity axis
    .sample("equal", n=12)                          # uniform-bins, count path
    .options(on_error="raise")
)

# Validate the output choice and estimate work before writing anything.
print(
    pipeline.output("out/run1", container="hdf5", dry_run=True,
                    inspect_sources=True).render()
)

result = pipeline.output("out/run1", container="hdf5")  # needs the [array] extra

output.text:
The output layer mirrors the input side: a declarative `OutputSpec` (what each timestep holds)
+ a pluggable `OutputEncoder` (where domain logic lives) + a generic `ShardWriter` (chunking,
short-policy, containers, manifests). Provider-backed `media:` columns are decoded generically;
application-derived tensors such as action bins remain encoder plugins.

## The output unit: a Track

A **track** is one entity's timestep sequence — the output unit (generalizing a per-POV
episode/clip). `tracks_from_ticks(schema, ticks, source_id)` produces one track per entity,
each record being that entity's fields at a timestep merged with the tick's globals. A
**shard** is a fixed-length chunk of a track.

jobs.text:
The `kur-*` CLIs run a whole pipeline from **one JSON document**. This page enumerates every
recognized key per job kind. The same information ships machine-readably as a JSON Schema:
`kur-validate --print-schema` dumps it (point your editor's `$schema` at it for autocomplete),
and `kur-validate job.json` preflights any job in milliseconds — no data read.

quickstart.text:
In this first run, kuration will examine six small sensor sessions, score 42 candidate windows,
select 12 windows that cover different activity and fault patterns, write training-ready NumPy
shards, and read one shard back. The example is deterministic, needs no download, and uses only
the SDK's NumPy core.

Expected time: under ten minutes including installation, and normally under one minute once the
package is installed.

quickstart_cmd.text:
## 2. Run the pipeline

```bash
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aintropy-solutions/kuration-sdk/main/examples/quickstart.py
python quickstart.py --out quickstart-out
```

narration.text: The README says it curates large Physical AI datasets into training-ready data.
It cuts raw clips or time-series data into windows, then keeps the useful ones.
The pipeline starts with input, then chains operators, then ends in terminals.
That flow turns candidate windows into selected data and verified artifacts.

narration.text: A typical chain windows data, filters bad windows, and samples evenly.
The same chain can dry-run first, then write the dataset when it looks right.
The quickstart example examines 42 candidate windows and selects 12.
It writes 12 shards and a reproducible config.json for the same run.
To try it, download the quickstart script and run python quickstart.py --out quickstart-out.
The documented output shows the preflight, the shard count, and the reproducible config path.
Pipelines are immutable, so every operator returns a new pipeline.
The artifact records schema, pipeline, and checksums, so replay stays auditable.
Clone the repo, run the quickstart, and inspect the shards.
If it helps your workflow, keep exploring the docs and examples.
